title: mcp
text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an AI agent, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, discover and call external tools. This module exposes fossick functions as MCP tools. The agent sees each tool’s name, arguments, and docstring. These docstrings tell the agent when to use each option. They define the tool interface and are longer than other fossick docstrings.
Most tools take the arguments of the Python function they wrap. They also take a limit on returned text, such as max_chars. A tool cuts a long result at that limit. It adds a note with the number of cut characters. The note tells an agent to ask for more. Tools convert results to plain JSON types before returning them. The server uses standard input and output by default.

text:
Reading the store
These methods are added to fastcdp’s Page. Each method returns plain data.
shop_prep injects SHOP_JS when the page has no copy of it. It returns the store platform: shopify, woocommerce, bigcommerce, magento, next, or generic.
shop_products lists the products on the page. Each product has a number in i. Use that number or the title to choose a product. On a product page, the main product comes first. The other products have the related mark.
shop_cart reads the cart item count and subtotal. It uses Shopify’s /cart.js when available. It reads the page for other stores. The source key identifies the source. shop_lines reads the cart lines from the cart page.
shop_blockers names blockers such as cookie-banner, location-required, login-required, captcha, and modal-open. shop_dismiss clicks cookie banners and closable pop-ups.
A request that cannot run raises ShopError. For example, a product number that is not on the page raises this error. The error lists the available choices.

text:
Actions that check their result
shop_add adds a product selected by number or title. It returns ok, how, the product, and the cart before and after readings.







ok
Meaning




True
A cart signal changed. A cart signal is the item count, subtotal, cart lines, or a new confirmation message. how names the signal as count, subtotal, lines, or the confirmation message.


False
Nothing changed. error gives the reason.


None
The page has no cart count or subtotal to compare. The add is not confirmed.



A title must match a product title exactly or occur within a product title. An exact match takes priority. A Shopify product can have variants such as sizes. When several variants are in stock and you pass no variant, shop_add returns need='variant' and the in-stock variants. It does not choose a variant. A product with one in-stock variant uses that variant.

title: shop
text:
Checkout forms
shop_fields lists every visible form field on the page. Each entry has the field number i, the label, the autocomplete token and the current value. A drop-down entry also lists its options. shop_fields never returns password values.
shop_fill fills a form from a profile dictionary. The standard keys are first_name, last_name, email, phone, address1, address2, city, state, postcode, country, company, notes and the card_* keys. match_fields decides which field each key goes into. It checks the field’s autocomplete token first, then its name or id, then its label. It uses the words in FIELD_MAP, which include Australian wording such as “suburb” and “postcode”. Each field is used for one key at most.
A numeric key, such as '7', fills field number 7 from shop_fields. Use it for choices that have no standard key, such as size or delivery time.
After the fill, shop_fill reads the form again and reports whether each field holds the value. shop_set sets one field by its number.
shop_fill(submit=...) clicks a button or link by its name after the fill. A name that matches PAY_RX, such as “Pay now” or “Place order”, needs confirm=True. Without it, shop_fill raises ShopError and fills nothing.

text:
Shop
The methods above are asynchronous and require a Page. Shop wraps them as synchronous methods with shorter names: platform, products, cart, cart_page, lines, add, set_qty, remove, fields, set, fill, blockers, dismiss, snapshot, and md. The return type depends on the method. platform, snapshot, and md return strings. The other listed methods return dictionaries or lists.
Shop also has goto, open, find, and search. search tries the store search URL, the Shopify search page, and the page search box in that order.
shop(url) opens a session. It connects to the debug Chrome and starts it when needed. It reuses a tab that an earlier shop call left open on the same store. With resume=True, it keeps that tab on its current page instead of going to url. The fossick shop --add 0 command uses this tab to act on results left by a previous --search command.

text:
Tests
The offline tests cover site hints, profile key matching, cart change detection, product selection by number or title, the payment button guard, and cart line lookup. The cells under Live stores need the debug Chrome and network access. The tests skip those cells.

assert site_hint('https://www.coles.com.au/search/products?q=milk')['cart'].endswith('/trolley')
assert site_hint('https://www.amazon.com.au/s?k=x')['search'] == 'https://www.amazon.com.au/s?k={q}'
assert site_hint('https://members.ceresfairfood.org.au/products/search')['note']
assert site_hint('https://some-random-shopify-store.com') == {}     # generic path, no hints needed


#: A checkout form with Australian terms, mixed autocomplete coverage, and decoy fields.
FORM = [
    dict(i=0, tag='input', type='search', name='q', id='', autocomplete=None, label='Search parts', options=None),
    dict(i=1, tag='input', type='email', name='customer[email]', id='e', autocomplete='email', label='Email address', options=None),
    dict(i=2, tag='input', type='text', name='firstName', id='', autocomplete='off', label='', options=None),
    dict(i=3, tag='input', type='text', name='ship[ln]', id='', autocomplete='family-name', label='Family name', options=None),
    dict(i=4, tag='input', type='tel', name='contact', id='', autocomplete='tel', label='Email or phone', options=None),
    dict(i=5, tag='input', type='text', name='address1', id='', autocomplete=None, label='Address', options=None),
    dict(i=6, tag='input', type='text', name='address2', id='', autocomplete=None, label='Address line 2', options=None),
    dict(i=7, tag='input', type='text', name='locality', id='', autocomplete='address-level2', label='Suburb', options=None),
    dict(i=8, tag='select', type='select-one', name='region', id='', autocomplete='address-level1', label='State / Territory',
         options=[dict(v='VIC', t='Victoria'), dict(v='NSW', t='New South Wales')]),
    dict(i=9, tag='input', type='text', name='zip', id='', autocomplete='postal-code', label='Postcode', options=None),
]
hit = match_fields(FORM, dict(email='a@b.co', first_name='Sam', last_name='Nguyen', phone='0400 000 111',
                              address1='12 Smith St', address2='Unit 3', city='Brunswick',
                              state='Victoria', postcode='3056'))
assert {k: v['i'] for k, v in hit.items()} == {'email': 1, 'first_name': 2, 'last_name': 3, 'phone': 4,
                                              'address1': 5, 'address2': 6, 'city': 7, 'state': 8, 'postcode': 9}
assert hit['city']['label'] == 'Suburb'          # Use the autocomplete token instead of the label.
assert hit['first_name']['name'] == 'firstName'  # Use the name when autocomplete is off.

# The autocomplete token takes priority over a misleading label.
assert _score(FORM[4], 'email') == 0 and _score(FORM[4], 'phone') == 100
assert _score(FORM[0], 'first_name') == 0        # The search box does not match this key.
# Each field is used once. Unmatched keys are reported.
assert len({v['i'] for v in hit.values()}) == len(hit)
assert match_fields(FORM, dict(card_cvc='123')) == {}


#: An explicit variant takes priority over the card variant id. An unmatched variant is rejected.
class _VPage:
    async def eval(self, js): return 'https://x/p' if js == 'location.href' else [dict(id='1', name='Small'), dict(id='2', name='Large')]
_card = dict(url='https://x/p', vid='1')
assert (await _variant_id(_VPage(), _card, 'Large'))[0] == '2'
assert (await _variant_id(_VPage(), _card, 'Huge'))[0] is None
assert (await _variant_id(_VPage(), _card, None))[0] == '1'
assert (await _variant_id(_VPage(), _card, 'L'))[0] is None   # Both names contain 'L', but neither equals it. The code does not guess.
assert (await _variant_id(_VPage(), _card, 'large'))[0] == '2'

class _XLPage:
    async def eval(self, js): return 'https://x/p' if js == 'location.href' else [dict(id='3', name='X-Large'), dict(id='4', name='Large')]
assert (await _variant_id(_XLPage(), _card, 'Large'))[0] == '4'   # An exact name takes priority over a name that contains it.
assert (await _variant_id(_XLPage(), _card, 'X-L'))[0] == '3'

class _NoVariants:
    async def shop_prep(self): return 'shopify'
    async def shop_products(self): return [dict(i=0, title='Tee', url='https://x/p', vid='1', add=True)]
    async def eval(self, js): return 'https://x/p' if js == 'location.href' else []
res = await Page.shop_add(_NoVariants(), 0, 1, 'Large')
assert res['ok'] is False and res['need'] == 'variant' and 'nothing was added' in res['error']


#: Verify that only an exposed cart signal change counts.
assert _changed(dict(count=0, subtotal=0), dict(count=1, subtotal=9.5)) == 'count'
assert _changed(dict(count=None, subtotal=10.0), dict(count=None, subtotal=19.5)) == 'subtotal'
assert _changed(dict(count=1, subtotal=9.5), dict(count=1, subtotal=9.5)) == ''
assert _changed(dict(count=1), dict(count=None)) == ''     # A blank reading is not progress.
assert _changed(dict(count=1, lines=[{'title': 'a', 'qty': 1}]),
                dict(count=1, lines=[{'title': 'a', 'qty': 1}, {'title': 'b', 'qty': 1}])) == 'lines'


#: Product selection does not guess. An invalid request raises an error and lists the available products.
ITEMS = [dict(i=0, title='Oil Filter Z145A', related=None), dict(i=1, title='Oil Filter Z411', related=None),
         dict(i=2, title='Oil Filter Z411 Twin Pack', related=None), dict(i=3, title='Oil Filter Z145A', related=True)]
assert _match(ITEMS, 1)['i'] == 1
assert _match(ITEMS, '1')['i'] == 1                        # A string index.
assert _match(ITEMS, 'Oil Filter Z411')['i'] == 1          # An exact title takes priority over a longer title.
assert _match(ITEMS, 'twin pack')['i'] == 2                # A case-insensitive substring.
assert _match(ITEMS, 'Oil Filter Z145A')['i'] == 0         # The product takes priority over the recommendation.
for bad in ('flux capacitor', 9):
    try:
        _match(ITEMS, bad)
        raise AssertionError(f'{bad!r} should not have matched')
    except ShopError as e: assert 'Z145A' in str(e) or 'page has 4' in str(e), e


#: The payment guard covers common checkout labels.
for label in ('Pay now', 'Place order', 'Complete order', 'Confirm purchase', 'Buy now', 'Submit order'):
    assert PAY_RX.search(label), label
for label in ('Continue to shipping', 'Save address', 'Apply discount', 'Update cart'):
    assert not PAY_RX.search(label), label


#: Line lookup and numeric fill keys report page values without guessing.
CART = dict(count=2, subtotal=13.0, lines=[dict(i=0, text='Apples', qty='2', qty_kind='select', remove=True),
                                           dict(i=1, text='Pears', qty='1', qty_kind=None, remove=True)])
assert _line(CART, 1)['text'] == 'Pears' and _line(CART, '0')['qty_kind'] == 'select'
try:
    _line(CART, 5)
    raise AssertionError('line 5 should not have resolved')
except ShopError as e: assert 'cart page shows 2' in str(e), e

#: A numeric profile key addresses a `fields()` index and does not use `FIELD_MAP`.
assert match_fields(FORM, {'7': 'Large', 'city': 'Brunswick'})['city']['i'] == 7   # '7' is a field index, not a profile key.
assert _origin('https://shop.example.com/collections/all?x=1') == 'https://shop.example.com'

s.search('tree runner')[:2]

r.get('need'), [v['name'] for v in (r.get('variants') or [])][:3]

s.cart(lines=True), s.set_qty(0, 1), s.remove(0)

title: shop
text:
Limits
fossick does not solve captchas. It never clicks a payment button unless the call passes confirm=True. Store pages change over time. The in-page script can stop finding a store’s controls. Every action checks the cart and reports what it found. It does not assume that a click worked.

title: Quality
text:
A search engine ranks pages by how well they match a query. That ranking does not show which pages are useful to read. A question about building rules in Australia can return five cost guides from one trade directory before the government page that sets the rules. A programming question can return sites that copy Stack Overflow answers.
This module reorders results before it downloads a page. It does four things:
research in fossick.search calls curate when curated=True. This is the default. It also uses plan and interleave. You can use each function with a list of result dictionaries that has an href or url.

title: Quality
section: Identify a site from a URL
text:
Identify a site from a URL
Two URLs belong to the same site when they share a registrable domain. This is the part of the name that someone registered. docs.python.org and www.python.org both belong to python.org. The registrable domain usually has the last two parts of the host name. Some registries sell names one level down. For example, bbc.co.uk and nsw.gov.au have three parts. MULTI_LABEL_SUFFIXES lists these registry endings for the countries that fossick handles. host returns a URL host name in lower case without www.. registrable_domain returns the site.

Use one key for each page
The same page can have several URLs. The URLs can differ by www., a trailing slash, or tracking parameters such as utm_source. norm_url reduces a URL to one key. It removes the scheme, www., the fragment, tracking parameters, a default port, and a trailing slash. It sorts the query parameters. title: Quality
text:
Match authority to the question
The best source depends on the question. A government site is authoritative for a law question. Documentation is authoritative for a library question. A forum is useful for user opinions. DOMAIN_RULES lists the sites to move up (boost) and down (demote) for each question kind. The kinds are docs, policy, release, security, and community.
domain_matches checks a host name against a rule. A rule has one of four forms:








Rule
Matches
Example




Ends in a dot
Host names that start with it
docs.


Starts with a dot
The ending itself and every host under it
.gov.au


Contains a /
Only the host name before the /, with no subdomains
github.com/advisories


Any other text
That domain and its subdomains
sec.gov



Only a rule that ends in a dot matches the start of a host name. openai.com.evil.example does not match openai.com. blocked_matches applies the last form to a blocked list.

Remove copycat sites
SPAM_MIRRORS lists sites that copy content from other sites. Examples include Stack Overflow scrapers and GitHub mirrors. These sites add nothing to the original. Several search engines can rank them highly because they target each engine.
drop_spam removes results from these sites and from domains in blocked. It returns the remaining results and the removed domains. allowed keeps a domain even when a list contains it. It also keeps subdomains of that domain.
A query that contains site:reddit.com already selects a site. site_domains returns the domains named by site: in a query. For this query, curate skips copycat removal and the per-site limit. curate still reorders results by authority.

text:
Split one question into searches
A question such as “I want to rebuild my garage in australia, cheap options, what is the regulation on it, material options” asks three things. One search for all three parts mostly finds pages about the first part. plan creates one search for each part.
plan removes openings such as “I want to” (LEAD_INS) and empty phrases (FILLER). It splits the rest at commas, semicolons, question marks, and words such as “and”. It adds the topic words from the first part to each later part. Each search still contains “garage australia”. The original question is always the first search.

[q]

interleave merges result lists from several searches. It takes one result from each list in turn. It keeps a page that several searches found only once. For a duplicate page, it joins the queries lists. This gives each question part its own sources. Merging by score would favour a general guide over a source that answers one part.

text:
Reorder results
authority_rerank moves results from sites that DOMAIN_RULES boosts for a question kind to the front. It moves results from sites that DOMAIN_RULES demotes towards the back. cap_per_domain keeps at most max_per results from each site near the top. It moves the remaining results to the end in their original order. A list with fewer than three results stays unchanged.
Neither function drops a result. Results that do not move keep their order. Both functions return the reordered list and a second value. authority_rerank returns a report dictionary with intent, applied, boosted, and demoted. cap_per_domain returns the number of results moved to the end.

title: Quality
text:
Count stories, not URLs
Ten results can represent one story. For example, nine sites can reprint one news agency report. cluster_sources groups results with the same norm_url key or with mostly shared text.
shingles returns the set of three-word sequences in a text. jaccard divides the overlap of two sets by their union. cluster_sources applies jaccard to the shingles from each result title and text. Two results with a similarity at or above threshold are one story. The default threshold is 0.6. The grouping is transitive. When A matches B and B matches C, all three results form one group. Each group uses its first input member as its name.
independence returns the groups with a score. The score rises with the number of separate stories and sites. The result also lists its limits. Two sites that rewrite one press release in their own words do not share enough text to form one group.

title: Quality

curate
curate runs these steps in order:

drop_spam removes copycat sites.
authority_rerank reorders by authority for the kind of question. classify reads the kind from the query, or you pass intent. intent=None skips this step.
cap_per_domain applies the per-site limit. max_per_domain=0 skips this step.
diversity describes the result.

A query with site: skips steps 1 and 3. curate returns the reordered results and a report of what each step did. With rerank=False it returns the results untouched. The report then has dropped=[], demoted=0 and authority=None, and still has intent and diversity.

Tests

# Test registrable domains, including three-label registries.
assert registrable_domain('https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html') == 'python.org'
assert registrable_domain('https://www.bbc.co.uk/news') == 'bbc.co.uk'
assert registrable_domain('https://planning.nsw.gov.au/x') == 'nsw.gov.au'
assert registrable_domain('https://wko.at/') == 'wko.at'
assert registrable_domain('https://x.com') == 'x.com' and registrable_domain('') == ''
assert registrable_domain('http://192.168.1.1/a') == '192.168.1.1'      # An IP address has no site prefix to strip.
assert host('https://WWW.Example.COM./p') == 'example.com'


# Test one key per page and sorted query parameters.
assert norm_url('https://www.x.com/a/?utm_source=t#frag') == norm_url('http://x.com/a')
assert norm_url('https://x.com/a') != norm_url('https://x.com/b')
assert norm_url('https://x.com/a?b=2&a=1') == norm_url('https://x.com/a?a=1&b=2')   # Query parameters are sorted.
assert norm_url('https://x.com:443/a') == norm_url('https://x.com/a')               # A default port is removed.
assert norm_url('https://x.com:8443/a') != norm_url('https://x.com/a')              # A non-default port stays.
assert norm_url('https://x.com/a?mkt_tok=z&_ga=1&keep=2') == norm_url('https://x.com/a?keep=2')


# Rule matching controls both security and ranking.
assert domain_matches('docs.python.org', 'docs.') and not domain_matches('notdocs.com', 'docs.')
assert domain_matches('planning.nsw.gov.au', '.gov.au')          # A suffix rule covers a whole registry.
assert domain_matches('gov.uk', '.gov.uk')                       # The rule also covers the registry itself.
assert domain_matches('abcb.gov.au', '.gov.au')
assert not domain_matches('hipages.com.au', '.gov.au')
assert domain_matches('sec.gov', 'sec.gov') and domain_matches('www.sec.gov', 'sec.gov')
assert not domain_matches('openai.com.evil.example', 'openai.com')   # A bare prefix must not match.
assert blocked_matches('de.newbedev.com', 'newbedev.com')
assert not blocked_matches('newbedev.com.evil.example', 'newbedev.com')


# Test intent detection and abstention.
assert classify('rebuild my garage in australia, what is the regulation on it') == 'policy'
assert classify('planning permission for a garage') == 'policy'
assert classify('latest Tailscale release notes') == 'release'
assert classify('python asyncio api reference') == 'docs'
assert classify('CVE-2024-1234 advisory') is None or classify('log4j vulnerability advisory') == 'security'
assert classify('what do people on reddit think of it') == 'community'
assert classify('best turntables under 1000 euro') is None          # says nothing -> no reranking
assert classify('reddit release notes') is None                     # says two things -> no reranking
assert classify('') is None and classify(None) is None


# Test copycat removal and explicit `site:` constraints.
_h = [dict(href='https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1', title='real'),
      dict(href='https://newbedev.com/questions/1', title='mirror'),
      dict(href='https://de.newbedev.com/q/1', title='mirror subdomain')]
_kept, _rm = drop_spam(_h)
assert [h['title'] for h in _kept] == ['real'] and _rm == ['de.newbedev.com', 'newbedev.com']
assert drop_spam(_h, allowed=['newbedev.com'])[0] == _h            # The allowed domain also keeps its subdomain.

assert site_domains('site:reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA best server') == ['reddit.com']
assert site_domains('plain query', include=['NSW.gov.au']) == ['nsw.gov.au']
_, _r = curate('site:reddit.com best local llm', [dict(href=f'https://reddit.com/{i}') for i in range(5)])
assert _r['site_constrained'] == ['reddit.com'] and _r['demoted'] == 0   # The site constraint prevents diversity changes.


# Test authority ranking with the garage query.
_garage = [dict(href='https://hipages.com.au/article/garage-cost', title='How much to build a garage'),
           dict(href='https://oneflare.com.au/costs/garage', title='Garage costs 2026'),
           dict(href='https://www.planning.nsw.gov.au/exempt-development', title='Exempt development'),
           dict(href='https://airtasker.com/garage', title='Get quotes'),
           dict(href='https://abcb.gov.au/ncc', title='National Construction Code')]
_out, _rep = curate('rebuild my garage in australia, what is the regulation on it', _garage)
assert _rep['intent'] == 'policy'
assert [host(_url(h)) for h in _out][:2] == ['planning.nsw.gov.au', 'abcb.gov.au'], [_url(h) for h in _out]
assert _rep['authority']['applied'] and _rep['authority']['top_before'] == 'hipages.com.au'

# Reranking drops nothing.
assert len(_out) == len(_garage)

# An unknown or absent intent does nothing.
assert authority_rerank(_garage, None)[0] == _garage
assert authority_rerank(_garage, 'nonsense')[1]['applied'] is False


# Test site caps and list diversity.
_mono = [dict(href=f'https://hipages.com.au/a/{i}', title='Garage cost guide', body='what a garage costs')
         for i in range(5)] + [dict(href='https://abcb.gov.au/ncc', title='NCC', body='construction code')]
_capped, _n = cap_per_domain(_mono, 2)
assert _n == 3 and [host(_url(h)) for h in _capped][:3] == ['hipages.com.au']*2 + ['abcb.gov.au']
assert len(_capped) == len(_mono)                                    # Results move. They are not dropped.

_d = diversity(_mono)
assert _d['n'] == 6 and _d['domains'] == 2
assert _d['dominant_domain'] == dict(domain='hipages.com.au', share=round(5/6, 4))
assert _d['near_dups'] > 0                                           # The five guides have similar text.
assert diversity([])['n'] == 0 and diversity([])['score'] == 0.0

# A diverse set scores higher than one dominated by one site.
_div = [dict(href=f'https://s{i}.com/a', title=f'topic {i}', body=f'quite different text number {i}')
        for i in range(6)]
assert diversity(_div)['score'] > _d['score']
assert snippet_similarity('one two three four', 'one two three four') == 1.0
assert snippet_similarity('too short', 'too short') == 0.0           # Fewer than three words provide no trigram evidence.


# Test empty and describe-only paths.
assert curate('anything', [])[0] == []
_h2 = [dict(href='https://a.com/1', title='t')]
assert curate('q', _h2, rerank=False)[0] is _h2                      # Describe-only mode does not change the list.
assert 'diversity' in curate('q', _h2, rerank=False)[1]
assert curate('q', _h2, intent=None)[1]['intent'] is None


# Test planning for one question with three parts.
_GARAGE = ('I want to rebuild my garage in australia, cheap options, '
           'what is the regulation on it, material options')
_p = plan(_GARAGE)
assert _p[0] == _GARAGE                                   # The original question stays first.
assert len(_p) == 4                                       # The result has the original and three parts.
assert any('regulation' in s for s in _p[1:]), _p
assert any('cheap' in s for s in _p[1:]) and any('material' in s for s in _p[1:]), _p
assert all('garage' in s and 'australia' in s for s in _p[1:]), _p   # The subject returns in each facet.
assert 'want' not in _p[1] and 'what' not in _p[1]        # Planning removes the lead-in and filler.

# Planning abstains when it cannot split safely.
assert plan('sqlite wal mode vs journal mode performance') == ['sqlite wal mode vs journal mode performance']
assert plan('garage cost') == ['garage cost']                        # This query is too short for two questions.
assert plan('site:reddit.com best local llm, cheap options') == ['site:reddit.com best local llm, cheap options']
assert plan(_GARAGE, max_queries=1) == [_GARAGE]                     # Planning is disabled explicitly.
assert plan('') == []
assert len(plan(_GARAGE, max_queries=2)) == 2                        # The query limit applies.

# A facet with no new words is not a search.
assert plan('rebuild my garage in australia, the garage, australia') == \
       ['rebuild my garage in australia, the garage, australia']

# A rewriter replaces the heuristic and keeps the original.
assert plan('anything at all here', rewrite=lambda q: ['one', 'two']) == ['anything at all here', 'one', 'two']


# Interleaving gives coverage.
# A general result must not outrank a specialist result.
_cost = [dict(href='https://hipages.com.au/guide', title='complete garage guide'),
         dict(href='https://oneflare.com.au/cost', title='costs')]
_reg  = [dict(href='https://hipages.com.au/guide', title='complete garage guide'),

assert len(_il) == 4                                      # The guide appears once.

# Ragged and empty lists are valid.
assert interleave([]) == [] and interleave([[], []]) == []
assert len(interleave([_cost, []])) == 2


# Test clustering, including transitive groups.
_wire = ('OpenAI said today that it is lowering prices for its newest model across all tiers, '
         'effective immediately for every API customer.')
_syn = [dict(href='https://a.invalid/x', title='OpenAI cuts prices', body=_wire),

        dict(href='https://c.invalid/z', title='OpenAI cuts prices', body=_wire),

             body='We are updating the per-token price of our newest model from today.')]

assert len(_cl) == 2, _cl                                  # Three copies form one group. The original forms another.
assert _cl[0]['size'] == 3 and _cl[1]['size'] == 1
assert _cl[0]['canonical'] == 'https://a.invalid/x'        # The first input member names the group.

_ind = independence(_syn)

assert _ind['method'] == 'url+text' and _ind['confidence'] == 'medium'
assert _ind['limitations']                                 # The result lists its limits.

# transitivity: A~B and B~C is one family even where A and C alone fall short of the threshold
_chain = [dict(href='https://a.invalid/1', body='alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta'),
          dict(href='https://b.invalid/2', body='beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta iota'),
          dict(href='https://c.invalid/3', body='gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta iota kappa')]

# the same url twice is one source however differently it is described
assert len(cluster_sources([dict(href='https://x.com/a?utm_source=t', body='one two three four'),
                            dict(href='http://www.x.com/a', body='utterly different words here')])) == 1

_div = [dict(href=f'https://s{i}.invalid/a', body=f'entirely separate subject number {i} here')
        for i in range(5)]
assert independence(_div)['sources'] == 5 and independence(_div)['score'] > independence(_syn)['score']

_bare = [dict(href='https://a.invalid/1'), dict(href='https://b.invalid/2')]
assert independence(_bare)['method'] == 'url' and independence(_bare)['confidence'] == 'low'
assert any('too little text' in l for l in independence(_bare)['limitations'])
assert independence([]) == dict(n=0, sources=0, score=0.0, clusters=[], method='none',

text:
Turning HTML into markdown
A downloaded page contains markup that a reader does not need, such as navigation bars, scripts, styles and advertisements. to_md removes this markup and returns markdown. It accepts an HTML string or a response from fetch. With sel, it converts only the part that matches a CSS selector, such as sel='article'. html2md converts an HTML string. html_title returns the document title.

    multi:bool=False, # Return all selector matches joined together
    wrap_tag:str=None, # Wrap each multi-result in <wrap_tag>...</wrap_tag> when multi=True
    ignore_links:bool=True, ignore_images:bool=False,
    readability:bool=True, # False keeps the whole document; None keeps it when the article is too short
)->str:
Convert a fetched response or HTML string to markdown.

    s:str, ignore_links:bool=True, ignore_images:bool=False,
    readability:bool=True, # True extracts the article; False converts the whole document; None uses the whole document below `WHOLE_BELOW`

Convert HTML string s to markdown.

html_title
def html_title(
    s:str
)->str:
Return the document title, its first <h1>, or an empty string.


By default, to_md and html2md use readability. This article extractor finds the main article and removes the surrounding content. It can also remove content that you need, such as section headings. Pass readability=False for a saved page or a local HTML file. This converts the whole document. It removes scripts, styles, noscript blocks, template blocks and HTML comments. readability=None keeps the article when it has at least WHOLE_BELOW (200) characters. Otherwise, it converts the whole document. Use this setting when readability can remove almost all text, such as on a short documentation page or a link list. read uses the same readability setting for web pages. The test below shows that readability removes two <h3> headings that readability=False keeps.
html2md uses markdownify (MIT). Tables become GFM pipe tables. A code block is fenced and uses the language named by its class, such as language-yaml, lang-py or highlight-python3. The output does not contain <title> text. html_title returns that text. The tests below use six saved pages in fixtures/pages: an encyclopedia article, a documentation page, a blog post, a Q&A page, a rendered README and a news article.

_pages = {f.stem: f.read_text() for f in Path('fixtures/pages').glob('*.html')}
_w = {k: html2md(v, readability=False, ignore_links=False) for k, v in _pages.items()}
assert '| Part | Length | Height |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Arch span | 503 m | 134 m |' in _w['wiki']
assert '| Carries | Motor vehicles, trains, bicycles and pedestrians |\n| --- | --- |' in _w['wiki']   # a table with no <thead> gets a header row

text:
Downloading pages

Refusing private addresses
An AI agent can choose the URLs that a program fetches. Then a person can make the program fetch addresses inside your own network. Examples are the admin page of a router and the metadata service of a cloud server. A metadata service gives out credentials. This attack is called server-side request forgery. check_url refuses a URL that is not http or https. It refuses host names such as localhost and metadata.google.internal. It refuses a host that resolves to a private, loopback, link-local or other non-public address. For each refusal, it raises BlockedURL. The message names two ways to allow such a URL. To allow it for one call, pass allow_private=True. To allow it for the whole process, set the environment variable FOSSICK_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1. get_page, fetch, http_get and http_post run this check first. http_page does not run it.
local_host tells you if a host name or an address names this computer or the local network. It makes no network call. It returns True for these hosts:

localhost
a name that ends in .local, .lan, .internal, .localhost or .home.arpa
a name with no dot, such as intranet
an address that is not global, also in a short form such as 127.1

A program can use local_host to refuse a link before check_url looks up the name. check_url does not call local_host. Thus check_url allows a name with no dot when that name resolves to a public address.
The check looks up the host name. Then the download looks it up again. The two lookups can get different answers. A person who controls the DNS for a name can give a public address to the check and 127.0.0.1 to the download. This attack is called DNS rebinding. To stop it, the plain HTTP path of get_page gives libcurl the addresses that the check approved. It uses the libcurl option CURLOPT_RESOLVE. libcurl then connects only to those addresses. It does not look up the name again. The plain path also follows redirects itself. Before it connects to a new URL, it checks and pins the address of that URL in the same way. It does not send your cookies, auth or credential headers to a different host.
Some paths cannot pin the address. They keep only the first check. Through a proxy, the proxy looks up the name. This is also true for a proxy that the environment sets. The browser paths check only the first URL. These paths are heavy, stealthy, session, and auto=True after the plain step. The browser does its own lookups and follows redirects with no check. It also loads scripts and images from other addresses with no check. For URLs that you do not trust, use the plain path.

Downloading one page
get_page runs check_url. Then it downloads the page in one of four ways. By default, it sends a plain HTTP request. heavy=True loads the page in a headless browser, which runs the JavaScript of the page. stealthy=True uses the stealth browser of scrapling. This browser is made to pass bot checks, such as the checks of Cloudflare. session=True uses the logged-in Chrome of fossick.cdp, with its cookies. The browsers load on first use. When they cannot load, get_page raises BrowserUnavailable.
http_get and http_post are get_page with a set method and a 30 second timeout. All of them verify TLS certificates by default. Pass verify=False only for a host that you trust and that has a bad certificate. http_page sends a plain GET, POST, PUT or DELETE request. It does not run the address check. Use http_page only for URLs that your own code chose. Most callers need fetch, which comes next.
Two optional limits apply to the plain path. max_bytes stops the download when the body is larger than that number of bytes. Then it raises TooLarge. With this limit, a server that sends gigabytes cannot fill the memory before to_md runs. max_recv_speed sets the highest download speed, in bytes per second. Both limits are off by default. The browser paths do not use them. http_page also takes max_bytes. It takes curl_options for other libcurl options.
Some networks inspect TLS traffic with their own root certificate. curl_cffi does not use the system keychain. On such a network, the certificate check fails with curl: (60) ... unable to get local issuer certificate. To fix this, give the plain path a CA bundle file. The file must hold the normal roots and the inspection root. Pass the path of the file as ca_bundle= or verify=. Or set one of the environment variables SSL_CERT_FILE, CURL_CA_BUNDLE or REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE. fossick reads them in that order, on each request. It uses the first one that names a file.
On macOS, when none of these is set, fossick uses the system keychain. It reads the certificates of the system keychains with security find-certificate. It adds them to the roots of certifi. It keeps the result in its cache folder for one day. Thus an inspection root that your company put in the system keychain works with no setup. On other systems, when none of these is set, curl uses its own roots.
The bundle applies only when verification is on. Verification is on with verify=True, which http_get sets, or with ca_bundle=. fossick does not turn verification off by itself. Only verify=False from the caller turns it off.

fetch
Most code downloads a page with fetch. It calls get_page and returns the scrapling response object with two more attributes. html holds the page, or only the part that matches sel. xhr holds the background requests that fossick records when capture_xhr=True. The response also has status, url, and a json() method for JSON replies.
auto=True tries the download methods in this order:

plain HTTP
the headless browser
the stealth browser
the stealth browser through the logged-in Chrome

A bot wall is a page that asks for a verification step instead of the content that you asked for. auto=True stops at the first response that is not a bot wall. It records the method that worked in tier. When no method worked, tier is 'blocked'. It records each failed attempt and its reason in errs.
browser_session downloads many pages with one browser. A browser takes some seconds to start. browser_session keeps one browser open for the length of a with block. It gives you a function like fetch that uses this browser for each page.
auto=True can end in the logged-in Chrome. The last method connects to the debug Chrome on port 9223. It starts that Chrome when it is not running. It sends the cookies that Chrome has for the site. This is correct for a page that you want to read as yourself. It is not correct for a URL from a web page, a document or another person. Such a URL can make your logged-in browser open a page with your cookies.
When you do not trust the URL, pass auto=False. auto=False is the default for fetch. It is not the default for read. With auto=False, and without heavy, stealthy, session or capture_xhr, no function in this module starts a browser. No function connects to port 9223. This includes get_pdf and its proof-of-work step, read_arxiv, read_gh_file, crawl and read. The plain path always checks redirects. follow_redirects is 'safe' by default. fossick checks and pins each redirect itself. The section Fetching untrusted URLs, near the end of this notebook, tests this.
fetch can keep responses in memory. Three settings control this. All three are off by default. A call that does not set them sends a new request each time.

cache=900 keeps a response with status 200 in memory for 900 seconds. A later call with the same arguments returns the same response object, with no request. The memory keeps at most MEM_MOST (256) responses. When it is full, the response used longest ago goes first.
per_host=True sends one request at a time to each host. When two threads ask the same host, the second waits until the first has its response.
remember_blocks=(401, 403, 429) remembers a host that gave one of these statuses, for cache seconds. The call that gets the status returns the response as usual. A later call to that host raises BlockedURL at once, with no request. This setting needs cache.

forget() clears the kept responses, the hosts that refused, and the locks. It also clears the results that search(cache=) keeps.

def forget():
Clear the cached responses, searches, refused hosts and host locks.


The tests below give fetch a fake get_page, so they need no network. The fake records each request. It gives status 429 for one path. It can wait at a barrier, which lets a test see two requests at the same time.

from types import SimpleNamespace
_asked, _busy, _most, _gate, _real_get_page = [], [0], [0], [None], get_page
def get_page(url, **kw):
    _asked.append(url); _busy[0] += 1; _most[0] = max(_most[0], _busy[0])
    try:
        if _gate[0]: _gate[0].wait()
        else: time.sleep(0.05)
        return SimpleNamespace(status=429 if url.endswith('/busy') else 200, html_content='<p>hi</p>', url=url)
    finally: _busy[0] -= 1
_e = 'https://example.com'
try:
    forget()
    fetch(f'{_e}/a'); fetch(f'{_e}/a')                        # the defaults: no memory, a request each time
    test_eq((_asked, _mem['pages'], _mem['blocks']), ([f'{_e}/a'] * 2, {}, {}))

    _asked.clear()
    r1 = fetch(f'{_e}/a', cache=0.3); r2 = fetch(f'{_e}/a', cache=0.3)
    test_is(r1, r2); test_eq(len(_asked), 1)                  # a cache hit
    fetch(f'{_e}/a', timeout=5, cache=0.3); test_eq(len(_asked), 2)   # other arguments: another entry
    time.sleep(0.35); fetch(f'{_e}/a', cache=0.3); test_eq(len(_asked), 3)   # the time is over

    _asked.clear(); forget()
    _most_was, MEM_MOST = MEM_MOST, 2
    try:
        for u in ('x', 'y', 'x', 'z', 'x', 'y'): fetch(f'{_e}/{u}', cache=60)
        test_eq(_asked, [f'{_e}/{u}' for u in ('x', 'y', 'z', 'y')])   # x was used last, so y went first
    finally: MEM_MOST = _most_was

    _asked.clear(); forget()
    test_eq(fetch(f'{_e}/busy', cache=60, remember_blocks=(429,)).status, 429)   # the first 429 comes back as usual
    test_fail(lambda: fetch(f'{_e}/other', cache=60, remember_blocks=(429,)), contains='answered 429')
    test_eq(_asked, [f'{_e}/busy'])                           # no request for the second call
    fetch(f'https://example.org/other', cache=60, remember_blocks=(429,))   # another host is asked
    forget(); fetch(f'{_e}/other', cache=60, remember_blocks=(429,))       # forget() clears the refusal
    test_eq(len(_asked), 3); assert _mem['pages']
    forget(); test_eq((_mem['pages'], _mem['blocks'], _mem['hosts']), ({}, {}, {}))
    test_fail(lambda: fetch(f'{_e}/a', remember_blocks=(429,)), contains='needs cache')

    def _two(**kw):
        _most[0] = 0
        ts = [threading.Thread(target=fetch, args=(f'{_e}/{i}',), kwargs=kw) for i in range(2)]
        for t in ts: t.start()
        for t in ts: t.join()
        return _most[0]
    test_eq(_two(per_host=True), 1)                           # two threads on one host: one after the other
    _gate[0] = threading.Barrier(2, timeout=5)
    try: test_eq(_two(), 2)                                   # the control: with no per_host they overlap
    finally: _gate[0] = None
finally: get_page = _real_get_page; forget()



Bot walls
Many sites show a challenge page instead of their content when they think that the visitor is a script. Two common examples are the “Just a moment” page of Cloudflare and the Anubis proof-of-work page. The challenge often has status 200. Thus it looks like a successful download. fossick treats a response as blocked in three cases:

its status is 401, 403, 429, 503 or 530
its HTML contains the marker of a known challenge or captcha widget
it has status 200 and less than 200 characters of HTML

The tests below check these rules. They also check that a page which only contains the word captcha is not blocked.
The cells after the tests use real sites. The test run does not run them. They show these results:

fossick finds a Cloudflare wall and an Anubis wall.
auto=True stops at the plain tier for a page that needs no browser.
browser_session uses one browser for two pages.
session=True downloads through the logged-in Chrome.

assert cf.status == 403, f'expected a Cloudflare 403 challenge, got {cf.status}'
assert _blocked(cf) is True            # fetch(auto=True) escalates from here (heavy -> stealthy -> session)
print('cloudflare:', cf.status, '| blocked?', _blocked(cf))

print('anubis wall detected by _blocked?', _blocked(an))

wiki = fetch('https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anubis', verify=False)

plain = fetch('https://example.com', auto=True, verify=False)

text:
Crawling and batches
crawl visits pages breadth-first. It starts at one URL and follows links that match follow_sel. It stops after visiting max_pages pages. By default, it stays on the starting site. It returns responses with status 200. It reports and skips a page that it cannot download. delay waits between requests. Use it to reduce the load on a small site. For crawls with heavy or stealthy, one browser stays open for the whole crawl unless reuse=False.
keep filters links before it adds them to the queue. It receives each link as an absolute URL. The URL uses the page address after redirects. Return True to queue the link. Use keep to limit a crawl to one site folder. crawl always reads the start page.

A server can read the last path as ../secret. The keep function accepts a link only when it stays in the folder after the redirect and has no .., including percent-encoded ...

from urllib.parse import unquote

class _FakePage:
    "Enough of a scrapling response for `crawl`: `url`, `status`, `css` and `urljoin`."
    def __init__(self, url, html): self.url, self.status, self.html, self._s = url, 200, html, Selector(html)
    def css(self, q): return self._s.css(q)
    def urljoin(self, href): return urljoin(self.url, href)

_g = 'https://docs.example.com/en-us/guide/'
_links = ''.join(f'<a href="{h}">x</a>' for h in ('intro', 'setup/', '/en-us/guide/api', '%2e%2e/secret', '../../blog/x', 'https://other.example.com/x'))
_site = {'https://docs.example.com/old/': (_g, _links)}   # a redirect to another folder
_asked, _real_fetch = [], fetch
def fetch(url, **kw):
    _asked.append(url)
    final, html = _site.get(url, (url, '<p>leaf</p>'))
    return _FakePage(final, html)
def _in_folder(u): return u.startswith(_g) and '..' not in unquote(unquote(u)).split('/')
try:
    test_eq(len(crawl('https://docs.example.com/old/', keep=_in_folder)), 4)
    test_eq(_asked, ['https://docs.example.com/old/', _g+'intro', _g+'setup/', _g+'api'])
    _asked.clear(); crawl('https://docs.example.com/old/')   # no keep: every link on the site is queued
    assert _g+'%2e%2e/secret' in _asked and 'https://docs.example.com/blog/x' in _asked

text:
PDFs and arXiv papers
get_pdf downloads a PDF, or reads one from disk. It returns a PdfDocument from pdf_oxide. It returns None when the bytes are not a PDF. It looks for the %PDF- signature in the first 1024 bytes of the content. It does not look at the URL. Thus it accepts arXiv papers, which have URLs with no .pdf ending. is_pdf is the same check for bytes that you already have.
The NCBI PubMed Central archive puts a small proof-of-work check in front of its PDFs. When the reply is such a check, get_pdf solves it. Then it downloads the PDF again with the answer. Any page can contain the markers of this check. Thus the second download uses the plain path of get_page. It has the same address checks, redirect checks, timeout and max_bytes as the first download.
max_bytes limits the size of the PDF. When save_path is a folder or a file name, get_pdf saves a copy of the file there. The examples download two papers from the Self-Determination Theory site and show the start of their text.

arXiv HTML, with the maths
arXiv shows most new papers as HTML pages made by LaTeXML from TeX source. read_arxiv_html reads this page with one fetch. It uses plain HTTP by default. It returns title, text, figures and url. In text, each formula uses TeX. Inline formulas use $…$. Block formulas use $$…$$. A PDF can show the same formula as loose symbols, such as “1 dk”.
arxiv_md converts the page. It first replaces each formula with a token. This prevents the markdown conversion from changing the TeX. It then replaces each token with its TeX. A numbered equation becomes one line with its number. LaTeXML puts numbered equations in a table. The conversion escapes $ in the text as \$. This prevents it from starting a formula. The conversion removes scripts, styles, forms, menus and the table of contents.
figures contains up to 30 image links from the paper’s HTML folder. The paths contain no .., including percent-encoded values. read_arxiv_html returns None in these cases:

an error
a status other than 200
a page outside arxiv.org after redirects
a page that is not a LaTeXML paper
text shorter than 200 characters

Then read the PDF. read(target, html=True) does this for an arXiv target. It reads the HTML page first. It reads the PDF when no HTML page exists.
The tests use a saved, shortened LaTeXML page and a fake fetch, so they need no network.

text:
GitHub
gh_clone returns a local repository copy. The first call clones it into fossick’s cache folder, in a folder named owner__repo. It uses HTTPS and does not ask for a password. Pass ssh=True to try SSH after HTTPS. Use this for a private repository with an SSH key. SSH uses batch mode and fails at once when it needs a passphrase. The clone contains only the latest commit. Pass depth=None for the full history, or pass another commit count. timeout limits each git command in seconds. When git exceeds this limit, fossick stops git, removes the incomplete folder and raises TimeoutError. Later calls fetch the clone and reset it to the latest commit. Git uses /dev/null as stdin and does not read the caller’s terminal. fossick gives git a separate environment and does not change os.environ. It refuses a target that starts with -. It puts -- before the URL, so git cannot read the URL as an option. gh_clone returns a local path unchanged. Code that accepts a repository also accepts a local folder. read_gh_repo reads files from that clone and returns {path: text}. By default, it reads the README, pyproject.toml and every Python file. It caches the results for one hour. read_gh_file downloads one file as raw text from its GitHub page URL. It returns the source exactly as written. It converts the file to markdown only when GitHub serves HTML.
gh_repo reads a repository’s owner/name from a github.com link. It also reads links to files, issues and commits, SSH remotes, and the owner/name shorthand. It makes no network call. It does not check that the repository exists. The shorthand matches any text with that form, such as and/or. A program that reads prose must filter the result.

These tests give gh_clone a fake subprocess.run, so they need no network. By default the clone is HTTPS only and shallow, and -- comes before the URL. A failed HTTPS clone does not try SSH, because SSH can ask for a passphrase. With ssh=True, SSH comes second and runs in batch mode. Git gets its own environment, and os.environ stays the same. A clone that passes timeout raises TimeoutError and leaves no folder. A target that starts with - is refused before git runs.

from unittest.mock import patch
import uuid


_runs = []
def _fake_git(fail=(), slow=False):
    def run(cmd, **kw):
        _runs.append((cmd, kw))
        if cmd[1] == 'clone':
            d = Path(cmd[-1]); d.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); (d/'half').write_text('x')
            if slow: raise subprocess.TimeoutExpired(cmd, kw['timeout'])
            if any(f in cmd[-2] for f in fail): return subprocess.CompletedProcess(cmd, 128, '', 'fatal: no access')
        return subprocess.CompletedProcess(cmd, 0, '', '')
    return run

_url = f'https://github.com/fossick-test/{uuid.uuid4().hex}'
_d = _clone_dir(_gh_remotes(_url)[0])
_before = dict(os.environ)
with patch('subprocess.run', _fake_git(fail=('https://',))):
    test_fail(lambda: gh_clone(_url), contains='no access')
test_eq(len(_runs), 1)                                        # HTTPS only: no SSH fallback
cmd, kw = _runs[0]
test_eq(cmd, ['git', 'clone', '--depth', '1', '--', _gh_remotes(_url)[0], str(_d)])
test_eq(kw['env']['GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT'], '0'); test_eq(kw['timeout'], 300); test_eq(kw['stdin'], subprocess.DEVNULL)
assert not _d.exists()                                        # the failed clone left nothing behind
test_eq(dict(os.environ), _before)                            # os.environ is never changed

_runs.clear()
with patch('subprocess.run', _fake_git(fail=('https://',))): test_eq(gh_clone(_url, depth=None, ssh=True), _d)
test_eq([c[2:] for c, _ in _runs], [['--', _gh_remotes(_url)[0], str(_d)], ['--', _gh_remotes(_url, ssh=True)[1], str(_d)]])
assert _gh_remotes(_url, ssh=True)[1].startswith('git@github.com:')
assert 'BatchMode=yes' in _runs[1][1]['env']['GIT_SSH_COMMAND']
shutil.rmtree(_d)

_runs.clear()
with patch('subprocess.run', _fake_git(slow=True)): test_fail(lambda: gh_clone(_url, timeout=5), contains='more than 5')
test_eq(_runs[0][1]['timeout'], 5)
assert not _d.exists()                                        # stopped git, removed the part-made folder

_runs.clear()
with patch('subprocess.run', _fake_git()):
    test_fail(lambda: gh_clone('--upload-pack=touch /tmp/x'), contains='starts with "-"')
test_eq(_runs, [])
test_eq(_gh_remotes('git@github.com:a/b.git'), ['https://github.com/a/b.git'])   # an SSH address clones over HTTPS too

section: Finding the API behind a page
text:
Finding the API behind a page
Many modern pages are almost empty when they arrive. Then JavaScript loads their data with background requests. These requests are called XHR or fetch calls. They usually return JSON. You can read that JSON directly instead of the rendered page.
find_xhr loads a page in a headless browser and records the background requests that the page makes. It returns each request whose URL matches pattern. Each result is a dictionary with url, content_type and the decoded data. With session=True, find_xhr records the requests through the logged-in Chrome. Then each result also has a capture.
replay_xhr sends a captured request again as a plain HTTP call with the cookies of the browser. Use it to call an API that needs a login, with no open browser.
pattern can be a regular expression, such as .*products.*, or a shell-style glob, such as *products*. compile_pattern accepts both forms. It first tries the text as a regular expression. If that fails, it treats the text as a glob.

compile_pattern
def compile_pattern(
    pattern
):
Compile pattern as a regular expression, or as a shell-style glob such as *foo* when it is not a valid one.



assert compile_pattern('.*products.*').search('https://api.example.com/products?q=1')
assert compile_pattern('*products*').search('https://api.example.com/products?q=1')
assert not compile_pattern('*products*').search('https://api.example.com/search')

An API rarely returns records at the top level of its JSON. Records can be under results or several levels down at data.products.items. json_records searches the whole payload for the longest list of dictionaries. With with_key=True, it also returns the key that holds the list.
paginate_api reads every page of a paged JSON API. It sends the request repeatedly and increases the page number in page_field. It stops when a page is empty, shorter than the page size, or follows max_pages pages. It finds records with results_field when you provide one. Otherwise, it uses json_records. With save=True, it writes each page to a file. A later run reads the saved pages instead of fetching them.

text:
YouTube
These three functions use yt-dlp. search_yt searches YouTube and returns result dictionaries. read_yt returns one video’s details and its transcript under source. The transcript comes from YouTube’s English automatic captions. A video without captions has an empty transcript. With read_yt(url, cues=True), read_yt also returns cues. This list contains {start, end, text} entries with times in seconds. yt_link(url, seconds) makes a watch link that opens at the given time. read_yt caches results and cues on disk by video id. download_yt saves audio as mp3 or video as mp4. The mp3 format needs ffmpeg. All three accept verify=False to skip certificate checks. Use this option behind a proxy that rewrites HTTPS.

text:
One function for every source
read accepts each kind of target that the readers above accept. For each target, it returns the same seven fields: ok, kind, title, source, text, skipped and meta. Thus a program can treat all targets in the same way. This includes web pages, PDFs, arXiv papers, YouTube videos, GitHub content and local files.
what_is finds the reader for a target. An arXiv id is a new id such as 1706.03762, an old id such as hep-th/9901001, or an arxiv: id. A path that exists on disk wins over every URL rule. Thus a folder named hep-th/9901001 is a folder. A local file named pdf is read from disk, not fetched. A GitHub URL that contains /blob/ is one file (ghfile). Other GitHub URLs are a repository (github). Any other http or https URL is a web page. A failed read returns ok=False with the reason in skipped. read raises ValueError only for a target that is none of these kinds.
To find arXiv and YouTube links, what_is reads the host of a URL. It does not search the full text of the URL. Thus https://docs.example.dev/youtube.com-guide is a web page, not a YouTube video.

text:
Fetching untrusted URLs
A program that reads links from web pages, documents or messages fetches URLs that another person can choose. For these URLs, call fetch, get_pdf and read with auto=False. fossick then uses only plain HTTP. It checks and pins each address, and checks each redirect again. max_bytes can limit the size of each download.
The tests below use a small web server in this process, on 127.0.0.1. The address check refuses 127.0.0.1, so _public_loopback makes the check count it as public for the length of a test. The server can then act as a site on the internet. _public_loopback can also give a name an address that only the check sees. libcurl does not see that address.
Any page can contain the proof-of-work markers that get_pdf looks for. Here, the page contains them. The answer redirects to localhost. get_pdf refuses this redirect. The server log shows that it did not send the request to /secret.

_Site.hits.clear()
with _public_loopback(): test_fail(lambda: get_pdf(f'{_base}/paper.pdf'), contains='localhost is an internal host')
test_eq(_Site.hits, ['/paper.pdf', '/paper.pdf'])   # the answer was sent; the redirect to /secret was not followed

fossick checks a redirect by the address to which its host resolves. It does not check only the host name. Here, inside.invalid resolves to 10.0.0.7, so fossick refuses the redirect. The second fetch tests address pinning. Names that end in .invalid never resolve in real DNS. The fetch can reach the server only through the address that the check approved and gave to libcurl.

_Site.hits.clear()
with _public_loopback({'inside.invalid': '10.0.0.7'}):
    test_fail(lambda: fetch(f'{_base}/to-inside'), contains='resolves to 10.0.0.7')
with _public_loopback({'pinned.invalid': '127.0.0.1'}):
    r = fetch(f'http://pinned.invalid:{_srv.server_port}/page')
test_eq(r.status, 200)
test_eq(_Site.hits, ['/to-inside', '/page'])

read(readability=None) returns the whole page when readability keeps almost no content. The page /links contains a list of links, which readability removes.

max_bytes stops a large response body. The server sends 4 MB without Content-Length. fetch and get_pdf stop after 100,000 bytes and raise TooLarge. Without max_bytes, the download has no size limit.

title: search
text:
search sends one query to several search engines and merges their results into one list. Each engine finds pages that other engines miss. A page that several engines rank highly usually gives a useful result. Fossick uses ddgs to reach the engines. ddgs does not need API keys. search merges the lists with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). It can then reorder the merged list by query relevance.
google loads the Google results page in a stealth browser. It is slower than search. research searches, downloads readable results, and returns a markdown digest with a citation for each source. You can pass the digest to a language model.

title: search
text:
The ddgs client
get_ddgs returns a shared DDGS client for each timeout and proxy setting. It creates each client on first use. ddgs_env reads proxy and certificate settings from the environment. This supports search behind a corporate proxy. It reads the proxy from DDGS_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY or https_proxy. It reads a certificate bundle from FOSSICK_CA_BUNDLE, SSL_CERT_FILE, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE or CURL_CA_BUNDLE.

Asking each engine
For text search, Fossick queries each engine in TEXT_BACKENDS separately. It keeps each engine’s results in that engine’s rank order. It does not use ddgs combined search. That search picks engines at random and favours Wikipedia. backends lists every ddgs engine for a category. When pages is greater than 1, Fossick asks each engine for that many result pages. It drops results on later pages when they repeat earlier results. The test checks that ranks continue across pages.

text:
Merging the lists
Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists without using the engines’ own scores. The scores are not comparable. Each page gets 1/(k + rank) from each list that contains it. RRF adds these values. A page ranked first scores more than a page ranked eighth. A page found by several engines gets one value from each engine. k is 60 by default. It controls how much more the top ranks count than the lower ranks.
rrf treats two URLs as the same page when they differ only in scheme, www., a trailing slash or tracking parameters. It uses norm_url from fossick.quality. For each page, it keeps the longest snippet. It also keeps the fused score and engines, which lists the engines that found the page.

text:
Reranking
Search engines use more than exact query words when they rank results. rerank reorders results by how well their title, snippet and URL match the query. It combines this relevance score with the merged score. mix sets the weight of the merged score. Its default is 0.4. A value of 1 ignores the reranker. When method is not 'none', rerank adds a rerank field with the relevance score.
method selects the scorer. 'lexical' uses BM25, a standard word-matching formula. bm25 computes scores from the result list. It does not need a stored index. 'flashrank' uses the small cross-encoder model from flashrank. The model reads the query and each result together. It matches meaning better. It needs pip install flashrank. flashrank_scores returns None when flashrank is missing. method='flashrank' then raises ImportError. 'auto' uses flashrank when installed and BM25 otherwise. 'none', the default for search, keeps the merged order.

text:
Where and when
The best answer to many questions depends on the country. Building rules, prices and availability differ by country. Search engines use a country-language region code, such as au-en. The default region='auto' reads both parts from the query.
infer_country looks for country names, adjectives and cities in COUNTRY_WORDS. It answers only when the query names one country. A query that names two countries returns None. infer_language counts common function words in LANG_WORDS, such as “the” and “what” or “der” and “und”. It answers only when one language has the highest count and at least two matches. infer_region joins the country and language results. A query with no language signal uses the country’s usual language from COUNTRY_LANG. The default us-en fills any part that the query does not define. An English question about France gives fr-en.
timelimit keeps only recent results. Use 'd', 'w', 'm' or 'y' for the past day, week, month or year.

text:
search
search is the main entry point. For text, it queries every engine in TEXT_BACKENDS in parallel. It merges the lists with RRF and reranks them with method. backend='google' restricts it to one engine. n cuts the final list only. It does not change the number of engines queried. Increase pages to get more candidates. With fuse=False, and for the images, news and books categories, it uses ddgs search for that category. The videos category uses search_yt to search YouTube.
An empty query returns an empty list without using the network. When every engine fails, search prints one warning per process and returns an empty list. text, images, news, videos and books are search with a category set. extract downloads one URL with ddgs. It returns {url, content}. The default content format is markdown.
cache=900 keeps a result in memory for 900 seconds. A later call with the same arguments returns that result without a request. An empty result is not kept. This prevents an outage result from being kept. fetch(cache=) uses the same memory and the MEM_MOST limit. forget() clears the memory. The default cache=0 asks the engines on every call.

text:
research
research turns a question into readable sources in five steps:

plan, from fossick.quality, splits a question with several parts into one search per part. It keeps the original question as the first search.
Each search uses search, or google when engine='google'. research interleaves the results by taking one result from each search in turn.
The default curated=True makes curate remove sites that copy other sites. It also moves authoritative sources up. research drops copycats before it downloads pages.
research downloads candidates in order with fetch(auto=True). Each batch contains as many pages as needed to reach n. It stops after it gets n pages with at least 400 characters of readable markdown. A failed, blocked or short page goes into dropped with its reason. The next candidate replaces it.
With focused=True, focus reduces each page to about chars characters from passages that best answer the question.

It returns a dictionary with query, sources, digest, dropped, region, curation and plan. Each source contains its title, href, working fetch tier, publication date, answered queries and markdown in md. The digest joins the sources with ---. Each source has its title, URL, publication date when known and the question part it answers.
page_date, usable and focus also work on their own. page_date finds a page’s publication date and returns YYYY-MM-DD, or None. It reads JSON-LD data, <meta> tags named in DATE_META, a <time> element or a /2018/09/ URL. usable checks for a 200 response, no bot wall and at least min_chars characters of readable markdown. min_chars=0 skips the length check. focus keeps passages that answer a query. It keeps opening blocks within 30% of the character budget. It then adds the highest-scoring blocks. It returns them in their original order and uses … for gaps.
The next cell tests paging with stand-in engines.

title: fossick
text:
fossick gets text from the web and puts it into Python programs. You can give it a search query, a URL, an arXiv id, a YouTube link, a GitHub repository, or a local file. It returns markdown that a person or a language model can read. AI agents can use it to look up information. Its functions return plain data such as strings, lists, and dictionaries. You can print this data or pass it to a model.
search sends a query to several search engines at once. It merges their answers into one ranked list. read takes one target and returns its text. fetch downloads a page. to_md converts its HTML to markdown. Some sites refuse downloads from scripts. fetch can also load a page in a headless browser, a stealth browser, or a copy of Chrome where you are logged in. cdp_connect drives that Chrome for pages that need clicks or typing. You can also use these functions from the shell with the fossick command. Agents can call them through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

text:
One function for every source
Use read when you have a target and want its text. read first calls what_is to classify the target. The result is the name of a reader:

dir for a local folder
file for a local file
arxiv for an arXiv URL or id
youtube for a YouTube link
github for a repository
ghfile for a file on GitHub
pdf for a URL that ends in .pdf or /pdf
web for any other http or https URL

A path that exists on disk wins over every URL rule.
read returns the same seven fields for every supported target:







field
holds




ok
True when the reader produced content


kind
the reader used, one of the names above


title
the title, or the first heading of the text


source
the URL, or the absolute path of a local file


text
the content as markdown


skipped
why nothing was read, when ok is False


meta
details from that reader, such as the authors of a paper or the HTTP status of a page, and the time it was read



Here read opens this repository’s own README:

target = str(repo_root()/'README.md')
assert what_is(target) == 'file'
result = read(target)
assert sorted(result) == ['kind', 'meta', 'ok', 'skipped', 'source', 'text', 'title']
assert (result.ok, result.kind, result.title) == (True, 'file', 'fossick')
assert '# fossick' in result.text and result.skipped is None
result.kind, result.title, result.ok

A folder or GitHub repository contains multiple files. read does not combine them into one document. It returns ok=True with empty text and the local path in meta['path']. You choose which files to open. For a GitHub repository, that path is a fresh clone in fossick’s cache. With pages=True, a PDF returns a list of (page_index, text) pairs. Page indexes start at 0.
Sometimes a recognised target produces no content. A site can serve a bot check instead of the page. A YouTube video can have no English captions. A URL that looks like a PDF can return another file type. read reports these cases with ok=False and a reason in skipped. It does not raise. It raises ValueError only when the target is not one of the supported kinds.

A logged-in Chrome
Some pages are shown only to logged-in users. fossick uses a separate copy of Chrome with remote debugging on port 9223. It uses the profile at ~/.cache/fastcdp/cdp-chrome. cdp_connect starts Chrome the first time it is needed. Log in to a site once in that window. The profile keeps the cookies. Later calls such as fetch(url, session=True) use the logged-in session. fetch(url, auto=True) and read use this Chrome when every other method is blocked.

title: fossick
text:
Untrusted URLs
fetch(url, auto=True) and read can use the logged-in Chrome on port 9223. read uses auto=True by default. This step starts Chrome when it is not running and sends its cookies for the site. Use this mode only for URLs that you chose. When a URL comes from a web page, document, or another person, pass auto=False:
fetch(url, auto=False, max_bytes=20_000_000)   # plain HTTP only; stop after 20 MB
read(url, auto=False, max_bytes=20_000_000)    # also for PDFs, arXiv papers and GitHub files
With auto=False, fossick does not start a browser or connect to port 9223. This also applies to PDFs and redirects. The plain path refuses private and local addresses. It connects only to the checked address. A second DNS answer cannot send it to 127.0.0.1. It checks each redirect in the same way. max_bytes and max_recv_speed limit download size and speed. Both limits are off by default. Through a proxy and in browser paths, fossick checks only the first URL.
On a machine that inspects TLS traffic with its own root certificate, curl_cffi does not trust that root. It does not use the system keychain. A download then fails with curl: (60) ... unable to get local issuer certificate. Set SSL_CERT_FILE to a CA bundle file that holds the normal roots and the inspection root. For example, run export SSL_CERT_FILE=~/Library/Java/macos-all-ca.pem. fossick also reads CURL_CA_BUNDLE and REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE. You can pass ca_bundle= on each call. Verification stays on.

text:
Acting on a page
An agent needs to know which page elements it can click or edit. The HTML of a full page is too long to read. snapshot builds a short view from the accessibility tree. Screen readers use this tree to describe the page. Each control becomes one line, [#id] role "name", such as [#42] button "Add to cart". Chrome assigns the id to the element. With interactive=False, snapshot also lists headings, forms and other landmarks.
type_text clears a field before it types. fastcdp’s fill_text adds text to the existing field value. click_settle clicks and waits for the page to settle. It does not fail when a click on a single-page app does not navigate.
fill_form takes a dictionary of {label: value}. It finds each field by its visible label or name. It types into text fields and selects options in drop-downs. With submit, it clicks the button or link with that name. It returns a new snapshot. It raises ValueError when no field matches a label or no button or link matches submit.

Action

text:
Screenshots and annotation
collect gathers screenshots while a person browses. It adds a bar with capture and done buttons to the page. Each capture hides the bar before it takes a screenshot.
collect stops when one of these events occurs:

The person presses done.
count screenshots have been taken.
tout seconds have passed.
The stop event is set.

With every_n, collect also takes a screenshot every every_n seconds without a button press. With save_dir, collect saves each screenshot there as a PNG file named from prefix. The default prefix is the page title. It returns a list of (image, path) pairs. Without save_dir, it returns a list of images.
BUTTON_JS, HIDE and SHOW draw, hide and show the bar.

annotate lets a person point to page elements. The page outlines and numbers each clicked element. An agent can use this information to ask which button or field the person means.
annotate ends when the person presses done, tout seconds pass or the stop event is set. It then takes a screenshot with the numbers. It returns (img, selected). selected is a list with one dictionary for each element. Each dictionary has the keys n, role, name and selector (a CSS selector). With save_dir, annotate also saves the screenshot as a PNG file named from prefix.
